extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of philosophy of science, mathematicians, and readers interested in scientific method and logic
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and explanatory rules for judging scientific reasoning, when a science is deductive rather than experimental, and how inductions and definitions function in mathematical demonstration. Includes concrete formulæ used in geometric proofs and guidance about model-making and simplifying hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of general reasoning (use of distinguishing marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, from observation of certain known particulars, what was seen to be true of them can be inferred to be true of any others, it may be inferred of all others which are of a certain description; we therefore determine once for all what are the distinguishing marks by which such cases may be recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General propositions act as formulæ recording the criteria (marks) by which we decide when an induction legitimately extends to a new case. The process is identification of an object and ascertaining it has those marks, either directly or via other marks collected by previous inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat general propositions as formulae for particular-to-particular inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive general propositions are not intermediate steps in reasoning but mere formulæ for inferring particulars from particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real premises are the individual observations; general propositions are records of the criteria used in past inductions so that future cases can be recognized as falling within them. Whether we identify the new case by the marks themselves or by marks of those marks, the inference is from particulars to particulars conforming to the stored formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect induction via marks-of-marks (chaining inductions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new instance may be brought within the scope of an induction indirectly by first recognizing a mark of it, then recognizing that mark as itself a mark of another property, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the government example: perceived testimony (mark) ⟶ acting in a manner (mark of mark) ⟶ desire of public good (mark) ⟶ likelihood of escaping revolution. Trains of reasoning can be long; each step is an induction even in a deductive chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple chains to infer complex conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: When several distinct marks each indicate different intermediate properties, their conjunction may serve as a mark for a further property; many physical and mathematical deductions consist of multiple chains united at the extremity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from optics: (1) rays on reflecting surface ⟶ angle of reflection, (2) parabolic surface ⟶ equal angles relative to focus, (3) parallel rays ⟶ angle of incidence equal to one of those equal angles; together these yield reflection through focus. In general, join several simple inductions to reach complex hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulæ for inferring equality and inequality in geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated basic formulæ used to infer equality or inequality of magnitudes: for equality — things which coincide are equals; things equal to the same thing are equals; a whole and the sum of its parts are equals; sums of equal things are equals; differences of equal things are equals. For inequality — a whole and its parts are unequals; sums of equal and unequal things are unequals; differences of equal and unequal things are unequals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the foundational marks by which geometrical equality/inequality is recognized. Proving propositions (e.g., base angles of an isosceles triangle equal) requires bringing the case within one of these formulæ, often by ingenious constructions that exhibit angles as differences or sums satisfying the formulæ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty and requirement of ingenuity in demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when the basic inductions (formulæ/axioms) are obvious, substantial scientific ingenuity may be necessary to recognize that a particular case comes within them by appropriate constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid's proof of base angles equality illustrates that one must imagine and select suitable pairs of angles (out of many possible) so that each pair's difference yields the angles in question and the pairs possess marks (like coincidence) required by the formulæ; this selection is non-obvious and requires cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms and definitions as few, simple inductions (marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The axioms and some definitions of a science are the simple inductions (marks) from which deductions are built by artful combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the marks are few and familiar, much of the difficulty and bulk of a deductive science consists in the connecting processes (combining marks) to bring unforeseen cases under these inductions. Strive to reduce foundations to the fewest simplest inductions to maximize deductive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion distinguishing deductive and experimental sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: A science is experimental in proportion as new cases need new observations (fresh inductions); it is deductive in proportion as it can draw conclusions about new kinds of cases by combining existing inductions to bring those cases under old formulæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The generic distinction hinges on whether marks-of-marks can be discovered to connect existing generalizations. Example: chemistry remains largely experimental because its generalizations are often detached; mechanics and geometry have become more deductive by finding connecting marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation of experimental into deductive science via connecting inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: A new induction that connects previously unlinked generalizations can turn an experimental science into a deductive one, either gradually or abruptly when a comprehensive induction bridges many propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton's discovery (unifying motions under centripetal force law) is the archetype: it connected many separate inductions at once and rendered formerly empirical truths deducible. Smaller-scale unifications occur continually but may leave the science largely experimental if many new unconnected truths arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of mathematics (science of number) in making sciences deductive
rubrics_metrics.description: Where variations of a qualitative phenomenon correspond regularly to variations of quantity, mathematical relations become applicable and render the theory of those qualities deductive to the extent of that correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate geometry and algebraization show that when qualities map to numerical relations, the deductive apparatus of mathematics (arithmetic, calculus) provides intermediate links (marks of marks) enabling indirect inferences. Use algebraization when possible to extend deductive reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simplified hypotheses and when to correct them
rubrics_metrics.description: For scientific convenience we may feign natural objects to be divested of properties irrelevant to the current inquiry (e.g., treat lines as without breadth); but these are hypotheses and depart from exact truth and must be corrected when the departures affect results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions in mathematics are convenient assumptions about idealized properties; they should be treated as hypotheses whose conclusions are only 'necessary' relative to those assumptions. When practical necessity arises, incorporate propositions about the aberrations or material properties to correct conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of mathematical necessity: conditional/hypothetical
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent necessity of mathematical truths arises from their correct deduction from chosen suppositions (definitions/axioms), which are themselves hypotheses; the necessity is conditional on the truth of those hypotheses, not absolute about the external world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that definitions like 'point without magnitude' or 'perfectly straight line' do not literally exist in nature; geometry's certainty is the certainty of reasoning from its hypotheses. For philosophical clarity, treat axioms as assumed generalizations rather than metaphysical necessities.
